key_finding: A nudge that shrouds the autopay-minimum option cuts minimum-only payment by 23% after six months but does not significantly reduce credit card debt, because liquidity-constrained cardholders shift toward slightly-higher autopay amounts or drop autopay and miss payments.
methodology: Field experiment on live credit card accounts with six-month follow-up; abstract-only for further design detail.
why_it_matters: Directly tests our support team's worry: a design change that clearly shifts nominal enrollment/behavior can leave the underlying financial outcome unchanged or worse for liquidity-constrained users — exactly the 'vanity enrolment' risk for round-up defaults, and shows anchoring near a floor value (minimum payment) can undercut intended gains.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not a savings product
does not address opt-in vs opt-out vs active choice framing directly, only a shrouding nudge
relevance_reason: Closest available consumer financial-product evidence that enrollment-shifting defaults do not necessarily change the underlying amount, with clear distributional heterogeneity by liquidity.

key_finding: Narrative overview of DC plan design summarizing effects of automatic enrollment and default investment options on participation, including potential negative effects on participant engagement.
methodology: Non-systematic literature overview, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides a recent synthesis of the employer-plan literature the brief flags as the closest large analogy, useful for background but not for the consumer self-directed decision itself.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
overview rather than primary evidence, no effect sizes given
relevance_reason: Recent state-of-the-art summary of the analogous employer-plan default literature.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment raises retirement participation short-term but induces passivity (low contribution anchoring, account churn) long-term, recommending auto-escalation and re-enrollment reminders as mitigations.
methodology: Narrative commentary/opinion article, abstract-only, no new data.
why_it_matters: Restates the passivity concern already better evidenced elsewhere in this set; low novelty and unclear rigor (zero citations, non-empirical).
limitations: employer retirement context
no original data or effect sizes
very new/low-visibility outlet
relevance_reason: Touches the passivity/engagement question but adds little beyond stronger papers already in the set.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for downstream (post-adoption) default effects, showing they depend on the time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs, and identifies gaps in current understanding.
methodology: Conceptual/theoretical synthesis and research-agenda paper; abstract-only for underlying study details.
why_it_matters: Tells us what to measure beyond the initial enrolment number — persistence, disengagement, and which moderators (preference strength, trade-off salience) determine whether a default helps or just relabels behavior; directly shapes what our 6–12 month measurement plan should track.
limitations: conceptual synthesis, not a quantitative effect-size estimate
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Gives the moderator framework needed to interpret whether enrolment gains from a default will persist or evaporate, which is the brief's central open question.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and utilization, and beneficiary passivity is highly insensitive even when the default option causes substantial welfare losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in Medicare Part D administrative data.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that passivity toward defaults can persist even when it is against the person's interest — cautionary evidence for defaulting-in on a financial product, but the setting (health insurance for low-income beneficiaries) is far from a self-directed banking app.
limitations: Medicare drug plan setting, not consumer finance
not a self-directed digital product context
relevance_reason: Rigorous natural-experiment evidence on default persistence and welfare harm to vulnerable groups, relevant to the distributional-risk question but off the brief's setting.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics substantially shrink the effect of automatic enrollment and default auto-escalation: steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of defaulted employees escalate on the first date, with further opt-out later.
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation, balance withdrawal on separation, and auto-escalation opt-out; abstract-only for full model detail.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: the enrolment lift from a default is real at signup but shrinks sharply once persistence and disengagement are tracked — the exact trade-off the brief asks us to resolve before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated mechanism does not map directly onto an app opt-out
relevance_reason: Directly supplies quantified evidence contradicting the premise that a default reliably and durably raises saving, which the brief explicitly asked us to find.

key_finding: Nationwide auto-enrollment in Germany's public pension system raised participation by 23 percentage points among low-income employees, but most individuals who were auto-enrolled actively opted out, with the default effect stronger when incentives were higher and knowledge of enrollment status lower.
methodology: Administrative and survey data linked around a nationwide policy introduction of auto-enrollment.
why_it_matters: A large, well-measured default effect size with clear heterogeneity by knowledge and incentive strength — useful benchmark for how much enrolment lift to expect, but from a public pension, not a consumer app.
limitations: public pension system, not consumer fintech
no data on amounts saved or long-run persistence beyond initial opt-out decision
relevance_reason: Provides a strong, recent default-effect size with heterogeneity analysis, though outside the consumer self-directed setting.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation/contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, are attenuated by 36 months, with only modest average savings increases at the longer horizon though inequality in savings is significantly reduced; a life-cycle model fits this with a ~$250 switching cost.
methodology: Data from over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly measures the persistence question the brief cares about most — default gains fade with horizon — and shows the main lasting benefit is reduced inequality rather than higher average saving, a distributional nuance for who is helped.
limitations: retirement plans with long horizons, not weeks-scale liquid savings
structural model estimates, not directly observed behavior
relevance_reason: Best available quantified evidence on how default-driven enrolment decays over medium-run horizons and who benefits from it.

key_finding: Across experiments including a five-country representative sample (n=4207), default nudges shift risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default (especially one the person refuses) lowers ratings of the advisor's honesty and advice quality, and how the default choice is framed (asking to invest vs. leave in cash) also shifts the amount allocated.
methodology: Multiple lab and large-sample field experiments on default framing in a wealth-management/investment-advice context.
why_it_matters: Directly speaks to the reputational and dark-pattern risk of defaulting users into a feature: a default that is later rejected or perceived as pushy measurably damages trust, which should shape how we frame and disclose the round-up default and exit path.
limitations: investment risk-taking with a wealth manager, not a round-up savings app
no long-run persistence data beyond the experimental session
relevance_reason: Directly evidences when a default reads as manipulative and damages trust — the EU consumer-protection/dark-pattern concern the brief flags — in a consumer financial-advice setting.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the default 2-3% contribution rate and the conservative default fund, with half still at the default after three years, largely offsetting participation gains against low default-rate anchoring, though it did raise saving in the lower tail of the distribution.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans, multi-year follow-up.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a pre-set default level anchors most participants for years, directly relevant to whether our pre-set multiplier will anchor people below what they would otherwise choose — but from an employer plan, so the magnitude may not transfer directly.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k), not a consumer app
no publication year given in metadata
predates the app/liquidity/regulatory context the brief flags as changed
relevance_reason: The foundational anchoring-on-default-level result the later consumer-facing literature is implicitly arguing with.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions finds default adherence arises from complementary deviation costs and opt-out costs (84% from their interaction), and adding an intermediate menu option captures 69% of achievable welfare gains at low revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on large-scale transaction data plus a stated-preference survey.
why_it_matters: Offers a mechanism (friction complementarity) for why consumers stick with a preset default versus an empty field, relevant to the level-anchoring decision, but the domain (tip menu presets) is a monetary choice, not a savings enrolment decision.
limitations: tipping decisions, not a savings or enrolment product
no employer-plan or fintech population studied
relevance_reason: Provides a rigorous mechanism-level account of how presets shape choice via friction rather than preference change, informing the preset-level design question by analogy.

key_finding: An opt-in payroll-deduction short-term savings account (withdrawable any time) at five UK firms saw very low take-up (≤0.7% of eligible employees ever activated), but among those who opted in, 96% still had a balance and 87% received a contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of a new choice-architecture program across five UK employers, with 12-month activation cohorts.
why_it_matters: The closest product match in the whole set — a short-term, liquid, withdrawable savings account — showing opt-in alone produces strong engagement among adopters but near-zero uptake, directly bearing on whether opt-in is sufficient for our feature; but the employer-payroll intermediary the brief says doesn't carry over is exactly the enrollment channel here.
limitations: employer-mediated payroll enrollment, the exact intermediary mechanism the brief says does not carry over
no opt-out or active-choice arm to compare against
relevance_reason: Structurally the nearest analog product (short-term liquid savings) and directly informs the opt-in disengagement-vs-uptake trade-off, despite the employer channel.

key_finding: A general theoretical characterization shows that when the designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, some form of weighted opt-out minimization (i.e., defaulting people in) is asymptotically optimal, with additional results for cases of disagreement, externalities, and normative ambiguity.
methodology: Formal welfare-economics model of optimal default design, validated via numerical simulation of asymptotic optima.
why_it_matters: Gives the theoretical conditions under which defaulting everyone in is actually optimal versus not — directly answering when our opt-out design is justified versus when it risks exploiting disagreement between what we want and what users want, which is the core normative question behind the entry decision.
limitations: pure theoretical/simulation exercise, no empirical population studied
abstract-only, no application to a specific financial product
relevance_reason: Supplies the formal decision-theoretic logic for when an opt-out default is welfare-optimal, directly informing the entry-mechanism choice rather than just describing an observed effect.

key_finding: Develops a taxonomy of six categories of autonomy violations used to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influences from dark patterns under existing and prospective EU law.
methodology: abstract-only; doctrinal/legal analysis mapping EU laws addressing dark patterns and proposing a normative autonomy-based classification.
why_it_matters: Gives the legal/reputational yardstick for whether an opt-out or pre-selected multiplier design would read as a manipulative dark pattern under EU law, directly bearing on how decision 1 and 2 should be implemented to stay defensible.
limitations: no empirical effect sizes on enrollment or saving behavior
not specific to financial products or fintech apps
doctrinal analysis rather than behavioral evidence
relevance_reason: Most direct treatment of the brief's explicit dark-pattern/manipulation risk concern in the relevant EU regulatory context.

key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, only 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (versus roughly 50% at lower defaults), and low-income employees were more likely to remain stuck at a likely suboptimal 12% default.
methodology: abstract-only; observational study of an employer retirement plan using an unusually high 12% default contribution rate, with literature comparison.
why_it_matters: Shows a high preset default can anchor people, especially lower-income ones, at a level that is not in their interest, echoing the anchoring risk for our round-up multiplier default, but in an employer-mediated plan.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
matching incentives differ from a round-up savings feature
abstract-only, limited detail on mechanism
relevance_reason: Direct evidence on default contribution level anchoring and heterogeneous opt-out behavior, though in the employer-pension analogy setting explicitly flagged as not carrying over.

key_finding: Abstract text is corrupted/unavailable; title indicates U.K. field experiments automating short-term payroll savings.
methodology: abstract-only; abstract text unusable ('Trant').
why_it_matters: Title suggests potentially relevant evidence on automating enrollment into short-term (liquid) savings, closer to our setting than pensions, but no usable content exists to assess any decision.
limitations: abstract is corrupted and provides no extractable findings
cannot verify methodology, sample, or effect sizes
relevance_reason: Potentially on-topic by title (short-term automated savings) but abstract gives no usable evidence.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment into just-in-time SMS overdraft alerts at major U.K. banks reduced unarranged overdraft charges by 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges by 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though alerts captured less than half of the achievable savings.
methodology: At-scale field experiments at major U.K. retail banks testing automatic enrollment into text-message alerts versus no alerts.
why_it_matters: The closest available precedent to our own decision: quantifies how default (auto-)enrollment into a discrete consumer banking-app feature changes real financial outcomes, and shows that even a well-targeted default only realizes part of the potential benefit — a caution against assuming enrollment numbers translate one-to-one into value delivered.
limitations: studies overdraft alerts, not round-up savings enrollment
outcome is charge avoidance, not saved amount
U.K.-specific banking regulatory context
relevance_reason: Nearly identical decision structure (default enrollment into a consumer banking-app feature) with measured, sizeable financial effect estimates.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrollment increased savings (£32-38/month per additional month enrolled) but was partially offset by increases in unsecured debt (£7/month) and higher mortgage uptake, with modestly improved credit scores and fewer defaults.
methodology: abstract-only; large-scale natural experiment from the staggered U.K. rollout of automatic pension enrollment to ~160,000 small employers.
why_it_matters: Warns that headline savings gains from default enrollment can be partly offset by compensating debt behavior, relevant to whether 'more people nominally saving' via round-up defaults translates into real net financial benefit.
limitations: employer-mediated pension plan, not liquid consumer savings
debt-offset dynamics may not transfer to a small round-up sweep
long observation window (41 months) not directly comparable to app engagement timescales
relevance_reason: Evidence that default-driven savings gains can be substantially offset elsewhere, cautioning against treating enrollment or nominal savings as a clean welfare gain.

key_finding: Adding a minor application 'ordeal' (removing auto-enrollment) to health insurance enrollment reduced enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people, undermining the standard efficiency rationale for such friction.
methodology: abstract-only; natural experiment studying removal of an auto-enrollment policy for public health insurance, with a selection-market model.
why_it_matters: Warns that adding friction akin to an active-choice screen can create adverse selection and disproportionately exclude vulnerable groups rather than efficiently screening out low-value enrollees — a distributional risk to weigh against active choice's engagement benefits.
limitations: public health insurance selection market, not consumer banking
adverse-selection dynamics may not apply to a savings feature with no insurance risk pooling
relevance_reason: Strong distributional evidence on who is excluded by added friction, directly relevant to the 'who is helped/hurt' question, in an off-domain selection market.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised campaign donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with larger effects on smaller donors and those with no prior default experience, and no compensating change in donation amounts.
methodology: abstract-only; staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting the timing of pre-checked recurring-donation defaults across political campaign websites.
why_it_matters: Near-identical mechanism to a pre-set round-up multiplier: shows a recurring-contribution default raises uptake but also produces disproportionate regret/refunds among smaller, less experienced users, directly speaking to the disengagement-and-complaints concern raised by the support team.
limitations: political donations, not a banking/savings product
refunds are a rough proxy for the disengagement/withdrawal outcomes we actually care about
relevance_reason: Closest available evidence that recurring-contribution defaults raise nominal uptake while also producing disproportionate regret among less-experienced, smaller users.

key_finding: A default option raises the reservation utility through a reference effect and self-selects those with better alternatives into active search; both effects are confirmed experimentally.
methodology: Lab experiment on optimal search with reference-dependent utility and a default option.
why_it_matters: Offers a theoretical mechanism for why letting users actively choose (versus defaulting them) can improve outcomes for those who search, background support for the active-choice option but not directly measuring financial enrollment.
limitations: abstract lab experiment, not a financial product setting
no enrollment, persistence, or amount-saved data
relevance_reason: General behavioral theory on defaults and search, useful background but distant from the consumer savings decision.

key_finding: Mandated active-choice browser screens under the EU Digital Markets Act increased alternative browser (Firefox) usage by 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects persisting at least 15 months.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered rollout of EU DMA-mandated browser choice screens across iOS and Android devices.
why_it_matters: Directly answers whether an EU-mandated active-choice screen produces large, durable behavior change relative to defaults in a consumer mobile setting — the core evidence needed for weighing active choice against opt-in/opt-out for onboarding.
limitations: studies browser choice, not a financial or savings feature
measures usage share, not disengagement, withdrawal, or amount-level outcomes
relevance_reason: Strongest available evidence that EU-mandated active choice produces large, persistent effects relative to defaults in a mobile consumer app context.

key_finding: A 'generalizable active privacy choice' interface design (opt-out without defaults) increased opt-out efficiency and reduced disruption; the least disruptive scheme left 98% of participants feeling undisrupted, a 40-point improvement over baseline schemes.
methodology: Usability study (n=410) testing nine non-default opt-out interface schemes implemented as a browser extension for privacy choice signals.
why_it_matters: Offers UI design principles for making a legally required non-default (active-choice-like) opt-out flow usable and low-friction, tangential guidance for designing our onboarding screen without it feeling punitive.
limitations: privacy-consent setting, not a financial or savings product
findings about generalizable opt-out choices may not transfer to a savings-level decision
relevance_reason: Provides interface design insight for non-default choice flows relevant to avoiding dark-pattern concerns, though outside the financial-product setting.

key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out raised sign-up rates and, for a single exam with stronger perceived endorsement, actual participation and pass rates, but only among students previously classified as 'responsive'; 'non-responsive' students showed increased sign-ups with no effect on actual outcomes.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up procedure from opt-in to opt-out across two university study programs.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates that opt-out defaults can raise nominal sign-up without changing effortful downstream behavior for disengaged users — precisely the support team's concern about vanity enrollment numbers — with clear heterogeneity by responsiveness.
limitations: university exam context, not a financial product
the target behavior requires ongoing effort rather than a one-time money sweep
relevance_reason: Best available field evidence that default effects on effortful downstream outcomes are concentrated among already-responsive individuals, directly bearing on the distributional/heterogeneity question.

key_finding: After the Pension Protection Act enabled target-date funds as default investment options, stock allocation became age-dependent following the TDF glidepath, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: abstract-only; account-level panel data on millions of U.S. middle-class retirement investors, 2006-2018.
why_it_matters: Suggests defaults can reshape where money is allocated much more than how much is contributed — relevant to whether a preset round-up multiplier would change amounts saved or merely default people into a level without changing effort.
limitations: employer retirement plan default concerns investment allocation, not a contribution-level or enrollment decision
long-horizon panel not comparable to app-engagement timescales
relevance_reason: Evidence that a default changed allocation composition far more than contribution amount, informing the anchoring/amount question in an off-domain retirement-investment setting.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT, all tested behavioral nudges — including default options — significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings in China, with the largest backfire effects from positive-narrative and default-option nudges, and meaningful heterogeneity by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey (n=220) testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on Chinese voluntary pension saving decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's 'defaults always help' premise by showing default nudges can backfire and reduce contribution willingness, with heterogeneous effects across demographic groups — exactly the kind of counter-example the brief asked to surface.
limitations: small sample (n=220) online survey, not a real financial product
Chinese cultural/institutional context differs sharply from EU consumer app
voluntary pension context rather than a liquid consumer savings app
relevance_reason: Provides an explicit, controlled contradiction of the 'defaults help' premise with reported heterogeneity, matching the brief's request for at least one contradicting paper.

key_finding: A pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians found people generally approve of financial nudges, with strong preferences for System 2-style, savings-framed interventions, while transparency had no significant effect on approval.
methodology: Pre-registered factorial survey experiment presenting 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios varying transparency, framing, and targeted cognitive system, n=2,100 representative Australian sample.
why_it_matters: Directly tests when a financial nudge is perceived as helpful versus manipulative, informing how we frame and disclose the round-up default to avoid the dark-pattern reputational risk the brief flags.
limitations: hypothetical scenarios, not an actual deployed product
measures stated approval/likelihood of use rather than real enrollment or persistence
general population, not specifically banking-app users
relevance_reason: Provides consumer-facing evidence on manipulation perception of financial defaults (C5), directly relevant to the EU dark-pattern risk the brief raises.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries a bank-account delivery option had no average effect on savings, but increased balances among those with previously nonpositive balances.
methodology: Field experiment/randomized offering among conditional cash transfer beneficiaries comparing cash versus bank-account delivery, tracking savings and trust outcomes.
why_it_matters: Suggests account-based savings mechanisms mainly help those with the least prior savings, a distributional nuance relevant to who benefits from a round-up default, though the population and mechanism differ substantially.
limitations: developing-country CCT population, not a self-directed consumer banking app user
not about enrolment design (opt-in/opt-out/active choice) but delivery channel choice
no long-term persistence data beyond initial measurement
relevance_reason: Offers some distributional evidence on savings-account effects for low-balance individuals, tangential to the enrolment-design question.

key_finding: Abstract fragment discusses an automatic IRA with an emergency (liquid) savings feature, comparing contribution and liquidity structures, but no results are stated.
methodology: abstract-only; design and outcomes not discernible from the fragment provided.
why_it_matters: Touches on pairing automatic enrolment with liquid emergency savings, conceptually close to a round-up pot, but the abstract gives no usable evidence.
limitations: abstract is a fragment lacking methodology or results
likely a state/employer-facilitated automatic IRA program, not a self-directed consumer app
relevance_reason: Topically adjacent (automatic enrolment plus liquid savings) but too little content to inform a decision.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrolment dramatically raised participation, and a substantial share of participants stuck to both the default contribution rate and default fund allocation, suggesting the default is read as implicit advice.
methodology: Before/after comparison of 401(k) elections at one large U.S. corporation following a shift from voluntary to automatic enrolment. Abstract-only for further detail.
why_it_matters: The classic 'power of suggestion' demonstration that a preset level anchors most users' choices — directly warns that whichever multiplier we pre-select will likely become the modal outcome.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer self-directed app
2001 data predates app-based, liquid, EU-regulated context the brief specifies
relevance_reason: Foundational anchoring-on-default-level evidence (C3) that the more recent literature responds to.

key_finding: Abstract unavailable; title indicates a comparison of savings behaviours between automatic and voluntary enrolment in a defined contribution plan.
methodology: abstract-only, no content provided.
why_it_matters: Directly on-topic title but no extractable evidence to act on.
limitations: no abstract or results available
employer-sponsored DC plan setting
relevance_reason: Topically matches the entry-decision question but cannot be evaluated from the given metadata.

key_finding: Institutional mistrust and minority/non-national status predict both under-saving and early withdrawal of retirement savings after a reform allowing early access, creating a 'double jeopardy' for vulnerable groups.
methodology: Analysis of three nationally representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension reform introducing an early-withdrawal option.
why_it_matters: Shows that some enrolled/defaulted savers withdraw early and that this risk concentrates among low-trust and minority users — directly relevant to the support team's worry that passive enrolment produces disengaged, complaint-prone users who withdraw quickly.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme in Estonia, not a consumer liquid-savings app
does not directly manipulate or compare enrolment designs (opt-in/opt-out/active choice)
relevance_reason: Provides distributional evidence on who withdraws savings early and disengages, informing which users a default could harm (C5, C2).

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, encouraging reflection on a hypothetical default-enrolment vaccination policy reduced stated vaccination intentions and lowered policy approval.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries testing effects of reflecting on a hypothetical default-nudge policy for booster vaccination.
why_it_matters: A cautionary counter-example showing defaults can backfire once made salient, useful context for weighing the manipulation/backlash risk of an opt-out design, though the domain is health policy rather than finance.
limitations: vaccination/health policy setting, not financial products
hypothetical scenario, not a deployed intervention
decision structure (one-off health choice) differs from ongoing app enrolment
relevance_reason: Analogous evidence that reflecting on defaults can trigger backlash, relevant to the manipulation-perception question but off-domain.

key_finding: Automatic enrolment and employer contributions are associated with higher likelihood of retirement plan participation among Millennials, while their absence predicts non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study, controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance, and assets.
why_it_matters: Reinforces the general default-participation link but adds little beyond more direct causal evidence already in the portfolio, and stays within the employer-plan setting the brief says doesn't transfer.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan context
correlational survey design, not causal identification
relevance_reason: Confirmatory but redundant evidence on default effects on enrolment, in an employer-plan setting.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic (passive) employer contributions substantially raised wealth accumulation, while tax subsidies requiring active choice raised total saving by only about 1 cent per dollar spent, because 85% of individuals are unresponsive 'passive savers' versus 15% wealthier 'active savers' who mainly shift assets across accounts.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel analysis of the full Danish population's response to retirement savings subsidies versus automatic employer contributions.
why_it_matters: The clearest large-sample evidence that passive defaults change real saved amounts while active-choice incentives mostly just relabel existing savings — a central data point for whether our default changes actual money saved or only nominal enrolment.
limitations: Danish tax-advantaged retirement account setting, not a consumer liquid-savings mobile app
effect driven partly by employer-mediated automatic contributions, the mechanism the brief says doesn't carry over
relevance_reason: Landmark active-vs-passive savings effect-size and heterogeneity evidence (C1, C5), though set in an employer/tax context.

key_finding: Active choice policies, and a novel 'enhanced active choice' design that highlights losses from the non-preferred option, can motivate behaviour change as an alternative or complement to automatic enrolment, especially where opt-out defaults are infeasible or ethically fraught.
methodology: A series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against standard default/opt-out approaches, referencing prior savings-behaviour applications.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether the active-choice entry design can capture much of the enrolment benefit without the ethical/reputational cost of opt-out, and offers a concrete 'enhanced' variant we could adapt for onboarding copy.
limitations: primary experimental application is medication adherence, not financial products
savings-behaviour evidence is referenced but not the central experiment reported
relevance_reason: The defining paper on active choice and an enhanced variant as an alternative to automatic enrolment (C6), central to the entry-mechanism decision.

key_finding: A broad synthesis of household financial behaviour identifies systematic empirical anomalies (savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, insurance) and catalogues the intervention types firms and governments use to address them, including choice architecture and defaults.
methodology: Narrative review/NBER book chapter synthesizing empirical and theoretical household finance literature on interventions including education, peer effects, product design, disclosure, and choice architecture.
why_it_matters: Gives a broad map of the choice-architecture toolkit beyond just defaults, letting us check whether product design or disclosure changes might address the enrolment/engagement trade-off better or alongside the entry-mechanism decision.
limitations: narrative overview, not a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
covers many topics beyond round-up-style consumer savings defaults specifically
relevance_reason: Serves as the review/synthesis-level source situating default and choice-architecture evidence within the broader household-finance literature, as the brief asks for.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrolment raised participation above 85%, and about 80% of new participants initially accepted both the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, with roughly half still at the default after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms comparing employee elections before and after automatic-enrolment adoption, tracked over several years.
why_it_matters: Directly measures how long a preset level anchors user choices (half still at default after three years), the closest available evidence on the risk that our pre-selected multiplier becomes the de facto ceiling for most users.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) setting rather than a consumer self-directed app
2001-era data predates modern fintech and EU regulatory context
relevance_reason: Directly measures persistence of anchoring on a preset default level over multiple years (C2, C3), core to the level-design decision.

key_finding: Randomized default enrolment in a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points, equivalent to a 50% matching incentive, driven by present bias and cognitive costs of decision-making, and increased subsequent active saving decisions.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among salaried employees in Afghanistan comparing default versus opt-in enrolment in a savings account, with follow-up mechanism experiments.
why_it_matters: Gives a clean causal effect size and mechanism (present bias, decision cost) for default enrolment, and evidence that defaults can shift subsequent voluntary saving behaviour, useful as a benchmark magnitude for our own default's likely lift.
limitations: salary-linked account facilitated via employer, not a self-directed consumer banking app
developing-country context differs from the EU consumer-protection regulatory environment
relevance_reason: Strong causal effect-size and mechanism evidence for default enrolment (C1), though the setting is employer-facilitated rather than a consumer app.

key_finding: A randomized nudge (payment reminders) in a Brazilian financial platform cut late-payment fees by 14% overall but raised overdraft fees by 9%, concentrated among users with a history of overdraft use, who saw a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Field experiment (RCT) with a consumer financial management platform in Brazil, measuring downstream fee outcomes across credit card and checking account behaviors.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, numbered demonstration that a well-intentioned consumer-finance nudge can help most users while causing net harm to a vulnerable subgroup — exactly the heterogeneity risk the brief flags for opt-out/default design, and argues for segmenting or monitoring outcomes by user type rather than reading aggregate enrolment or savings lift as sufficient evidence of success.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or round-up savings specifically
no direct measure of enrolment rate, anchoring, or active choice
single-market (Brazil) consumer credit context, not EU round-up savings
relevance_reason: Strongest available RCT evidence in this batch on distributional harm from a consumer-finance nudge, directly bearing on the brief's 'who is helped and who is hurt' concern.
